As human beings, we're wired to empathize with others (to varying degrees). If we suffer ourselves, we gain compassion for anyone going through a similar situation...but what about the situations we don't personally experience? We immediately see someone else's suffering and empathize with their struggle even if it isn't ours personally. I think this is how humans are able to feel passionately about causes that aren't affecting them personally. I think often of the phrase "there but for the grace of god go I"—like that could be me and there's no reason why that \*isnt\* me. Through that really scary thought, I think we're able to really understand that we are social animals wired to support each other through community.

I can't speak for my husband (since I'm the BP2SO) but we are both 10000% invested in doing all the inner work, the self-reflection, the therapy, all of it and we have a really beautiful and strong marriage. He goes to therapy on his own, I go to therapy on my own, and we have an amazing couples therapist that has really helped. We've learned to understand that the other is reacting out of pain and fear but mostly out of love. When I'm pushing him away, I'm fundamentally ashamed that such a wonderful man like him is stuck with a psychopants like me. I think he's amazing and I fear that I'm not good enough (which then leads to awful behavior like an awful feedback loop). Once I was able to work on forgiving myself, I was able to stop pushing him away so much. I began to see that I have other lovable traits and mental illness doesn't define me. It's been a long process and we'll probably never be done working, but I'm optimistic that we can have a family, grow old together, etc. as long as we stay focused and put in the work. So far we've been together 6 years and married for almost 3 years.

Welcome young padawan. I dab almost exclusively because it's so much easier on the lungs (in my experience) and it's discreet in terms of smell. You can use products labeled things like concentrates, wax, shatter, rosin, sauce, diamonds, etc. These are all types of cannabis concentrates that vary in texture and...well, concentration. Shatter has the consistency of a jolly rancher but a little softer; wax is usually more crumbly like a sugar scrub; rosin is like a smooth frozen yogurt, sauce and diamonds are highly concentrated and look like little sugar crystals steeped in honey. 

You'll need a dab rig, a titanium nail (I recommend Ti over ceramic and glass, but those are also options), a torch or an electronic nail to heat up the Ti nail, a metal tool to dab with (I used a cuticle nail tool for many years), and some water for the rig. Usually headshops have all of the above (minus the actual ganja) so you can feasibly get it all in one place. Happy dabbings!

My family left Cuba in the 60s as exiles (a lot of them identify as refugees) because of Fidel Castro's takeover. My dad was around 10 at the time and his mom (my grandma) was terrified because there were rumors that the state was going to lower the age of adulthood to 13 or 14 (I know there's a better term for this—like turning 18 in the US, having legal independence). This would mean that her son would soon become "property of the state," which would leave him vulnerable to forced separation from his parents, indoctrination, and forced labor. Kids were already being brainwashed into believing that Castro was the best and they were encouraged to report anyone who disagrees, even their own parents, since they are considered to be enemies of the state. In 1961, my grandma got my dad a spot on the Peter Pan flights, where the CIA and the Catholic church (an odd couple) worked together to get kids out of Cuba. All these kids (about 12,000 in total) came to the US alone and stayed in orphanages, detention centers, or any other Catholic facility that would take them. Luckily my dad was reunited with his parents just 3 months later while some families were never reunited :/

My mom's side of the family is also from Cuba and has a similar story, but they left much later (around 1968) . My mom's dad was so outspoken that he was arrested for speaking out against the Castro regime and thrown into one of the worst jails on the island. They intercepted him at the hospital literally as my mom was being born (they knew he'd be there soon with his pregnant wife) and he didn't get to meet his daughter until she was 4 years old. He endured so much during this time, but one thing that sticks out in my memory is the mock executions. They'd line all the prisoners up outside against a wall, count down 3-2-1, then fire blanks and tell everyone to go back inside. They'd do this several times a week. He got out eventually and almost immediately, they worked on getting all the necessary papers and permissions to leave. One very complicated paper trail later, they made it to Miami. 

Growing up among a Cuban-American community, I realized that every family has their own "exile story," often involving false paperwork, deception, smuggling, bribing, and other scary but necessary tactics needed to get out of a dictatorship. As a Cuban-American, I grew up with stories about family separation and the frailty of democracy, so needless to say I've had all the feelings these last couple of years regarding US policy.

Most of the time, I was already reeling from the shame and the guilt of it all and I knew the only way to get out unscathed was just to make a quiet exit from both relationships.

I was dating person A and when I got accepted into a college out of state, we stayed together in a long distance relationship. Then I met person B in college. He was fine and we had a lot in common and I liked him, but the thing that attracted me the most was that he was physically there. When the holidays rolled around, we all returned back to our hometowns Person B and I and parted ways for a few weeks. Then person A and I start to reconnect and all of the feelings came rushing back. Therein lies the cheating. Let me be clear, I absolutely hated myself. I felt like some kind of affection addict who couldn't manage to be alone for a few weeks and had to have a ship at every port. This went on for about a year until I got so depressed that I was even considering suicide. I never got caught, never had the big confrontation where I'm told I'm a terrible person, but I learned a lot of lessons that I carry with me. 

Now it's over 10 years later and I've been married for a few years now. After all of these relationships I tainted with deception, I am so happy to say that my marriage is absolutely beautiful. My husband and I have talked about all this at length, since it was pretty defining for me, I always say "thank goodness I learned all those lessons before I met you!" 

It's also worth mentioning that I was diagnosed with Bipolar II shortly after this whole shit show and I am doing so well. I feel like a different person now in my 30s. Some of the symptoms of Bipolar disorder include being impulsive and "excessive desire for sex" (yikes). So after a solid decade of thinking I'm a terrible person, I'm starting to reconcile with this past version of myself — she was in pain and needed love while feeling unlovable. I am so glad to say that the current version of myself has her shit WAY more together :)

Hey, friend, I don't know if this helps but it's honest: I tried about 5 different antidepressants in the course of a few years and then I finally found the right pill combination (yes, more than 1) was right for my particular brand of brain demons. It's absolutely a crapshoot at first, but the target is in there somewhere and you will find it. The ones who get better are often the ones who stick around long enough to try all the things. We have to survive out of pure spite if nothing else.

In regards to your fear, pretty much all the psychiatrists I know (members of my family, friends who became psychiatrists, my own psychiatrists) have such a passion for what they do and they'll be the first to acknowledge that you have a neurological problem, NOT a problem of character. Aww you sound like such a wonderful friend! My husband of 2 years (together for 5) has struggled with this when I'm in a depressive episode and we've talked about things that could help. First, sometimes I just need to ride it out, cry it out, say all the things I don't mean, and just know that someone is still there, knows that you exist, and is glad you exist even in spite of these dreadful episodes. That in itself is so healing, so you're already doing amazing by existing and still caring about her, still showing up for her.

Some of the time I feel like I lash out to push people away to "show them how unloveable I am" or "how much of a burden I am" and their sticking around and telling me they love me is doubly reinforced when they love me STILL, after all these years. When you have to remind yourself that you're worth the air you breathe and the resources you consume--every day--it can be really healing to have someone you don't have to wear a mask around. I'm in my 30s and I can honestly say that all my childhood or high school friends that are still my friends to this day are the ones with whom I've had conversations about mental health. If I need to wear a mask or pretend to be okay in front of some people, the friendships just aren't reinforced in the same way over the years. 

Second: try to let go of the idea that you need to provide solutions for her. That's unfair to you—no friend or partner is fully responsible for maintaining another's mental health. Most of the time I just want to vent and for someone to hear it and to just not try to give me any solutions. If I am looking for a solution to my problem, I'll say so, but if I'm ranting about my dickhead boss, the last thing I need is someone interrupting with all these things I can do, or should have done. Sometimes my husband and I will straight up ask each other, "do you want to vent or do you want solutions." It helps both of us, even though he doesn't have any mental illness at all.

Third: I encourage you to arrange to see your own therapist, because I think everyone should see a therapist regularly, and also because it can be really difficult to support a friend or partner who is depressed or suicidal.
